The expansion allows vertical software-as-a-service (SaaS) platforms, which serve businesses in specific industries, to offer Unipaas’ white-labelled payment solutions to Irish companies selling online. The move builds on Unipaas’ existing business in the UK. With white-labelled payments, SaaS platforms can offer card acceptance and payment services to their business customers under their own brand, with Unipaas providing the technology and J.P. Morgan Payments acting as the acquirer. The offering includes fraud controls and transaction routing designed to improve authorisation outcomes. According to J.P. Morgan Payments, collaborations with providers such as Unipaas help its clients navigate local regulations, meet customer expectations, and expand into new markets. David Avgi, Co-Founder and CEO of Unipaas, stated that the expansion into Ireland is driven by strong demand from both existing customers and the wider market. According to Avgi, the move allows Unipaas to support more vertical SaaS platforms and the businesses they serve with payment services designed to ensure continuity and simplify operations. He added that the company plans to keep developing its payment solutions as it expands further across Europe. Ludovic Houri, Head of EMEA and APAC for Merchant Services at J.P. Morgan Payments, described Ireland as an innovation-led economy and a natural next step in the company’s work with Unipaas. According to Houri, combining modern technology platforms with J.P. Morgan Payments’ acquiring capabilities in Europe creates a scalable foundation for commerce across the continent. Newly launched innovative solution, Receivables Matching, automates three-way matching across incoming payments, remittances, and open accounts receivables Cash application has historically been a necessary but often labor-intensive part of the receivables process. Once a payment arrives, accounts receivable teams must determine which invoices it belongs to, verify remittance information and resolve discrepancies before cash can be applied correctly. As businesses receive higher volumes of payments across a growing mix of payment types and channels, reconciliation has become increasingly complex. As a result, teams often spend valuable time manually moving between systems and matching data, instead of focusing on higher-value strategic work. To help clients streamline cash application, J.P. Morgan Payments has launched Receivables Matching, a solution that uses configurable matching technology to automatically match incoming payments, remittance information and open accounts receivable data. By bringing these data sources together, businesses can reduce manual effort, accelerate cash application, and improve visibility into receivables activity. "Receivables Matching simplifies one of the most complex and bifurcated parts of the receivables process by combining matching, exception management and reporting into one solution built entirely in-house by J.P. Morgan Payments. For clients, that means greater automation without having to replace the technology they already use, helping them operate more efficiently while gaining greater visibility into incoming cash flow," said Michelle Conklin, Head of Receivables and Public Sector, J.P. Morgan Payments. For companies managing large payment volumes, those efficiencies can have a meaningful impact. Grimco, a national distributor of sign, graphics and printing supplies, implemented Receivables Matching to help simplify its reconciliation process. After implementation, the company reduced manual review time by more than 60% and saw approximately 95% fewer errors requiring manual intervention. "Everyone on our team has been incredibly impressed with how quickly payments are posted now. That kind of speed and reliability has genuinely transformed how our AR team operates," said Donna Kirtian, Chief Financial Officer, Grimco. Receivables Matching is part of J.P. Morgan’s Receivables Online suite of reporting and reconciliation solutions. Receivables Online is a digital receivables management and account reconciliation solution accessed through J.P. Morgan Access® .  Receivables matching is currently available to clients in the U.S. and Canada. title: The S&P 500 may be headed for 'outsized gains' despite tech-stock rout, JPMorgan says - Business Insider
content: Amid a brutal week in the tech sector, the S&P 500 is flashing one sign better days are coming: improving market breadth. The tech sector is still getting pummeled by fears around AI, but JPMorgan Private Bank sees one bullish signal in the benchmark index that suggests the market is soon headed for a rebound. In a recent note, strategists at the bank pointed to increased market breadth, a measure of the number of winning stocks relative to losing stocks in the S&P 500. For a long time this year, breadth has been narrow, with just a few big names driving the gains at the index level while the majority of stocks struggled. The percentage of stocks in the index that have hit a new 20-day high has risen to over 50%. It's the first time market breadth has risen that high since the second quarter of 2025, around the time the market was making a historic comeback after the tariffs-fueled market crash. The extent to which market breadth has increased recently has historically been followed by more gains in the market over the next three-month and six-month periods, the bank added. JPMorgan recently lifted its year-end target for the S&P 500 to 8,000, implying 5% upside to the index's current levels. "Despite a crowded risk calendar, breadth and historical outperformance sets the US stock market up for outsized returns after the midterm elections," Kriti Gupta, an executive director and global investment strategist in JPMorgan's private bank arm, and Nick Roberts, a portfolio manager at the bank, wrote in a note on Friday. It's been a rough few weeks for US stock investors, with the S&P 500 and tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 on track to end October in the red amid several rounds of heavy selling in the AI trade. Fears around AI capex have been widespread and run in multiple directions: investors worry that Big Tech firms may be spending too much on artificial intelligence, and, on the other hand, fear that a pullback in spending could trigger a cascade of consequences that will crush suppliers in the data center space. Deteriorating market breadth was one of the first warnings investors got that not all was well with the AI trade. Several weeks ago, the benchmark indexes were hovering near record highs, but more than 80% of the S&P 500 had slipped into correction territory. The breadth decline was interpreted by strategists as damage building up underneath the market's surface. Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters. More analysts are eyeing a market as the market moves closer to the midterm elections, which has historically been a clearing event that allows stocks to renew their rally once its over. In the six months after the midterms, the S&P 500 has gained an average of 14% since 1970, according to an analysis from BlackRock. In the meantime, the tech sell-off continued on Friday as investors balked at Amazon's and Intel's latest earnings reports, with both tech giants signaling that capex spending would increase next year despite negative cash flow. The tech-heavy Nasdaq is down around 8% from its October peak. The iShares Semiconductor ETF, meanwhile, has plunged 28% from its 2026 high, while the Roundhill Neocloud ETF is down 43% from its latest peak.

Coinbase pays us for certain activity generated through this link. Prices displayed are informational. "The housing market is haunted," according to David Kelly, the chief global strategist at J.P. Morgan Asset Management. He lists the ghosts in his widely read Oct. 26 research note: more than a decade of too-easy money, tariffs, and immigration policies that raise the cost of building homes while limiting the number of people who need them, and a Fed whose rate swings hit housing harder than almost anything else. The one that should get the most attention is the people who aren't showing up. Kelly said he expects U.S. population growth of just 800,000 a year over the next few years. With an average household of about 2.5 people, he writes, that "implies a demographic need for just 320,000 new housing units per year," compared with roughly 1 million per year in the first two decades of this century. That cuts against the story most Americans have heard about housing: that the country simply hasn't built enough. Zillow estimated in July the U.S. was about 4.7 million homes short as of 2024, based on how many families are doubled up with unrelated people compared with how many homes sit vacant for rent or sale. Kelly's read is that the country is "still in a situation of net excess supply." Thursday's GDP report bore that out, Kelly told Fortune by email. Homebuilding fell again in the third quarter, "marking the 8th decline in residential construction in the last 10 quarters." But "the homebuilding decline is still relatively modest compared to the very fast increase in AI-related capital spending," he said. In the first 20 years of this century, Kelly wrote, the U.S. population grew by an average of 2.4 million people a year—about 1.5 million from births minus deaths and about 900,000 from net immigration. The natural increase peaked at 520,000 in 2025, he writes, and has likely resumed a steady decline as the population ages and birth rates fall. Immigration swung harder. Net international migration fell to 1.3 million in the year through July 2025 from 2.7 million a year earlier, and the Census Bureau projected it would be about 321,000 by July 2026 if trends continued. Kelly estimated that deportations are now almost canceling out legal net immigration, which is still positive but smaller. He said he expects that to hold "regardless of the outcome of the midterm elections," because enforcement is largely up to the administration, and Congress and the White House are unlikely to agree on an immigration reform bill. Kelly pointed to vacancies. Over the past four years, he writes, the rental vacancy rate rose from 5.6% to 7.3%, and the homeowner vacancy rate from 0.8% to 1.2%. Census figures released Wednesday put rental vacancy at 7.6% in the third quarter, up from 7.1% a year earlier. Between the second quarter of 2024 and the second quarter of 2026, he writes, the housing stock grew by about 2.8 million units. Buyers have thinned out. The National Association of Home Builders' measure of buyer traffic fell to 18 in October, its lowest level since April 2012 excluding the start of the pandemic, and 43% of builders cut prices. Kelly expects housing starts of 1.32 million this year, the weakest since 2019, falling to 1.24 million in 2027. Others see demand cooling, too. Harvard's Joint Center for Housing Studies said in June that household growth "has slowed sharply" and that reduced immigration is expected to dampen housing demand further. A Mortgage Bankers Association white paper projects 8.6 million new households from 2025 to 2035, down from 10.1 million in 2010 to 2020. Fewer buyers haven't meant cheaper mortgages. The 30-year fixed rate averaged 7.32% last week, according to Freddie Mac. Kelly notes that's below its 50-year average of 7.68%. From January 2008 to December 2021, the rate averaged just 4.15%. "It is important to recognize that this period was the anomaly, rather than today," he writes, and there's "little reason to believe that mortgage rates will fall much below 7.0%" without a recession. Kelly said he expects the Fed to raise rates in December and thinks weak housing could make that the last hike of this cycle. What would change his mind, he told Fortune, is if "wage growth suddenly picked up," or if inflation expectations priced into Treasury inflation-protected securities "were to rise significantly." Builders are squeezed from both sides. Construction workers are hard to find, Kelly writes, and wages in the industry are rising faster than elsewhere, partly because of the swing in immigration and partly because data-center construction is competing for the same workers. Tariffs and the same infrastructure boom have pushed up the cost of materials. Kelly told Fortune it's hard to put a number on how much the AI boom is adding to the cost of building a home. But spending on data centers rose 73% in the year through August, to an annual rate of $85 billion, he said, and "it is likely that the resource squeeze from data centers will intensify in 2027." The ghosts are hardest on the young. Homeownership has fallen since 2022, Kelly writes, "with a much sharper recent decline for those under age 35." He calls it a decline that is "postponing the reasonable aspirations of young people to be able to marry, settle down and build a family in their own home." Asked whether that drop is mostly about mortgage rates, Kelly pointed elsewhere. "I think it is a combination of tougher lending standards and the reality that older households have had more of a chance to accumulate a bigger down payment," he said. content: J.P. Morgan sees the coin as a better performer than stocks, though it comes at a cost. In its 2027 Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions report published in October 2026, J.P. Morgan projects that Bitcoin (BTC -2.15%) will return 10% annually over the next 10 years, versus its 7.5% forecast for large U.S. stocks. That call can be viewed as being very pessimistic about Bitcoin, as it's far lower than its compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 43.9% over the last four years, or as bullish, as it implies that it'll outperform every major asset class the bank models over a fairly long period of time. Given that framing, should you buy the coin and hold it through the bank's forecast period? J.P. Morgan expects 55% annual volatility for Bitcoin, and only 18% for large U.S. stocks. Both figures are broadly in line with the historical data. Using J.P. Morgan's figures for the coin's estimated forward returns versus stocks, the two earn the same 0.32 points of return above holding cash per point of volatility. That implies it does not really believe there will be a higher volatility-adjusted return with Bitcoin than with stocks, only that Bitcoin's higher expected return comes with proportionally more risk. The subtext here is that if you can't handle seeing the value of your investment swinging around a lot, Bitcoin is not going to be pleasant for you to hold even if it ultimately returns more. The factor at the heart of the projection is Bitcoin's shrinking rate of new supply being mined over time, versus the generally expanding global money supply. J.P. Morgan called the coin "a speculative asset and a hedge against monetary easing," meaning it's a risky asset that tends to do well when central banks expand the money supply. That mostly fits; while the coin hasn't proven it's an effective hedge against inflation, its strictly limited supply and the impossibility of printing more of it by fiat should mean its purchasing power continues to hold up over time. Per J.P. Morgan, this is the first time this report series has included a Bitcoin return forecast. It still doesn't recommend an allocation. Still, it expects Bitcoin to beat stocks over the next decade. So it's worth owning at least a little, once your traditional portfolio is sufficiently diversified. As for how much to buy, BlackRock found in December 2024 that a 2% Bitcoin allocation in a traditional 60/40 stock-and-bond portfolio accounted for 5% of its total risk, while a 4% allocation accounted for 14%. Morgan Stanley, on the other hand, suggested in late 2025 that the most aggressive portfolios should hold at most 4% in the asset. That argues for an allocation of less than 5% for most investors -- and remember, if the coin's inherent volatility is going to make you lose sleep, aim for the shallower end of that pool with your allocation. title: Why Did IMAX, JPM, CSX Stocks Surge To 52-Week Highs Last Week? - Stocktwits
content: Shares of IMAX Corp. (IMAX), JPMorgan Chase & Co. (JPM), and CSX Corp. (CSX) surged to 52-week highs on Friday amid a series of Wall Street price target hikes and continuing momentum from earnings results. IMAX stock closed down about 1.3% after jumping to an annual high amid Wall Street optimism, while JPM stock and CSX stock gained nearly 1% each at close. IMAX stock jumped to a 52-week high of $45.88 after it received a series of price target hikes on Friday following its strong second-quarter (Q2) earnings results. The theatre company posted revenue growth of 12.2% year-over-year to $102.8 million, while adjusted earnings per share jumped 65% to a record $0.43, topping analysts' estimates. IMAX said that it delivered its strongest Q2 global box office since 2019, generating $285 million as international markets outside China drove 24% growth. The company also reported its highest quarterly theatre installations in a decade and said strong early demand for Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey, including record opening weekend results and about $60 million in presales, positions it for a robust second half. Multiple analysts raised price targets on the company, summarized as below: On Stocktwits, retail sentiment was ‘bullish’ at the time of writing. IMAX shares have gained more than 20% this year. JPM stock jumped to a 52-week high of $353.37 on Friday, extending to four consecutive sessions in the green. Earlier this month, the bank posted strong quarterly results, declaring earnings per share (EPS) of $7.7 on revenue of $57.35 billion, much ahead of Wall Street expectations. It also reported its best quarter in terms of trading revenue, jumping 35% year-on-year to $12.1 billion. Investment banking fees came in at $3.3 billion, growing 30% in the quarter and rising to the highest level since 2021. JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon said every business segment posted record results, adding that market sentiment remains supportive of continued activity. JPM stock is up more than 8.5% this year, while retail sentiment has stayed ‘bearish’ over the past 24 hours. CSX stock jumped to an annual high of $53.40 on Friday, bolstering its weekly gains to 4.89%, the best since February. The company’s share prices climbed higher after it posted solid Q2 numbers, with revenue rising 10% year-on-year to a record $3.94 billion and diluted earnings per share increasing 23% to $0.54, beating Wall Street estimates. Net income climbed to $1 billion, while operating income rose 17% and the operating margin expanded 240 basis points to 38.3%, reflecting improved profitability. Citi raised the price target on CSX to $54 from $53 and maintained a Neutral rating on the shares, implying an upside of about 1.5% from its last close. Meanwhile, Deutsche Bank raised the price target on the company to $59 from $48 and kept a ‘Buy’ rating on the shares, implying an upside of nearly 11%. CSX shares have gained more than 46% in 2026. QuantumScape (QS), Paramount Skydance (PSKY), and Albertsons Companies (ACI) stocks dropped to new 52-week lows on Friday as investors punished delayed profits, merger execution, and weakening retail margins. QuantumScape stock declined over 4%, while Paramount Skydance and Albertsons stocks dropped over 3% each. QuantumScape stock reached a new 52-week low of $4.8 after investors reacted negatively to updated financial expectations surrounding its partnership with Volkswagen’s battery unit, PowerCo. Discovery (WBD) until June 1, 2027, or until a court decides on an antitrust case challenging the deal. The delay comes after California Attorney General Rob Bonta and 12 other states challenged the deal, saying the merger could hurt competition in movies, cable television, and streaming services, which may lead to higher costs for customers. Paramount executives said they still support the merger and believe the legal review will prove it can help audiences and creators. However, the court case may increase expenses and slow down the deal for both companies. Retail sentiment around the stock remained in ‘bullish’ territory. (IBRX) climbed over 2% overnight late Sunday as retail traders looked for signs that long-teased global partnership and expansion announcements could finally emerge ahead of the upcoming BTIG Virtual Biotechnology Conference between Tuesday and Wednesday. IBRX stock fell 4% on Friday to $7.10, snapping a two-session winning streak and extending its weekly decline to 19%. Retail chatter over the weekend centered heavily on the lack of July announcements and whether the silence could precede a larger update. One bullish trader noted that July had so far produced “zero posts” on global expansion or the Leonardo manufacturing platform and called it “the quietest month so far.” Despite the frustration, the user said the silence still felt like the “quiet before the kraken.” Another investor brought up founder Patrick Soon-Shiong’s comments, where he promised announcements on global expansion and partnerships. A third trader pointed to the narrowing July calendar and said that the upcoming conference could become a catalyst. Another bullish user urged patience, saying Soon-Shiong had been traveling globally and working on deals “behind the scenes,” adding: “Stay tuned…… the dots will get connected.” However, one user admitted being “disappointed” by the lack of news so far, but said that Soon-Shiong may have “good reasons for the delay.” Another trader speculated that ImmunityBio could issue a press release ahead of investor meetings if the company planned to discuss new information, and pointed to the company’s earlier $100 million raise for “global expansion.” A separate trader noted that the BTIG Virtual Biotechnology Conference runs July 28-29 and includes a bladder cancer session, but cautioned that “nothing is going to move this stock substantially until earnings or FDA approval.” The speculation comes against a broader strategy ImmunityBio has been building around its flagship immunotherapy Anktiva and its natural killer cell platform. Soon-Shiong has been focused on a long-term plan to create a “World Bank of NK Cells,” which is a scalable global supply of cryopreserved, off-the-shelf natural killer cells that could be rapidly distributed to patients and used alongside Anktiva. A major part of the effort involves automated manufacturing through the Nant Leonardo robotic system. In late June, Soon-Shiong posted an assembly update and said that the “world bank of NK cells” would be made available globally, adding that “global expansion [is] in motion.” ImmunityBio has also expanded Anktiva internationally, with regulatory and commercial progress across Europe, Saudi Arabia and other markets. In May, the FDA accepted ImmunityBio’s application seeking to expand Anktiva plus BCG into a broader group of patients with BCG-unresponsive non-muscle invasive bladder cancer, reversing an earlier refusal to review a similar filing. The agency set Jan.6, 2027, as the target date for a decision. ImmunityBio has said its Quilt-3.032 study showed 58% of high-risk papillary bladder cancer patients remained disease-free after 12 months, while more than 80% avoided bladder-removal surgery through three years of follow-up. Oracle Corp.’s stock rose 1.4% in overnight trading late Sunday and was the most-discussed ticker among retail traders on Stocktwits after a report said Nvidia was in talks to backstop a major OpenAI data center project. OpenAI is one of Oracle’s largest new customers, making the potential development a major tailwind for both companies. Oracle shares have faced pressure in recent months as investors scrutinize the mounting debt the company has taken on to build out data center capacity, much of it to support the cloud contracts with OpenAI. The Wall Street Journal reported Nvidia was in talks to provide a roughly $250 billion backstop for OpenAI as part of a massive data-center project. The guarantees from Nvidia would help the ChatGPT maker lease a 10-gigawatt project being developed by a unit of SoftBank in southern Ohio, the Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter. The ​power for the project is controlled by the U.S. government and funded separately by Japan under a ​recent trade deal, with U.S. Commerce Secretary ​Howard Lutnick involved in deciding who will receive access ‌to ⁠it, the reported added. Nvidia’s backing would allow the SoftBank unit to raise debt at more favorable terms than it could if OpenAI had no financial backer, since OpenAI has no investment-grade credit rating as an unprofitable private company, the report said. OpenAI is among the companies that have shown most interest in the site, while Anthropic, Microsoft and Google have also spoken to Lutnick about it in recent weeks, the report added. Oracle presents a compelling mix of opportunity and risk in the AI market, Stocktwits reported in an explainer on July 17. The stock is down 54% from its 2026 high on June 1 and 65% from its peak last September, making its valuation increasingly attractive. However, the pace at which the company has been piling on debt to fund new AI capacity – much of it tied to recently won business from OpenAI, whose competitive positioning and delayed IPO have come under scrutiny – has sharply increased Oracle’s risk profile. In that sense, Oracle’s future depends not only on its ability to execute – such as bringing additional cloud capacity online in a timely manner – but also on factors beyond its control. The second-quarter tech earnings, which are underway, would also have an impact on sentiment around AI and cloud, and potentially on Oracle’s stock as well. In fact, Oracle’s stock has slid for three sessions straight, losing about 10%, even after the company reported a major $7 billion software contract win from the U.S. Department of Defense last Thursday. S&P Global Ratings downgraded Oracle to BBB- on July 9, just a notch above junk, citing its rapidly growing AI-related spending. Oracle's five-year credit default swaps (CDS) have more than quadrupled since mid-2025 to a record about 203 basis points, meaning more investors expect Oracle to default on its loan, according to The Kobeissi Letter. Meanwhile, the Nvidia-OpenAI report drew a response from ace investor and Nvidia short Michael Burry. “Around and around we go. Nvidia to guarantee $200 billion of ChatGPT’s spending on $NVDA chips,” Burry wrote in an X post, referring to concerns of AI and cloud companies inking circular financing deals which some say significantly increase risks in the AI ecosystem. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for ORCL was ‘bullish,’ unchanged from the previous day. “$ORCL I am dreaming—If Jensen Huang or Elon Musk announce they would fully support Oracle’s data center expansion and provide financing guarantees, the stock could be back to $200 within three trading days,” a trader said, forecasting the stock nearly doubling. Another wrote: “$ORCL one thing the market seems to agree on: if OpenAI wins, Oracle wins.” For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com. Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) is reportedly in discussions to support a $250 billion financing package tied to an AI data center campus that OpenAI is considering leasing in southern Ohio. The development, backed by interests affiliated with SoftBank Group, could eventually represent the largest announced AI data center complex, with total investment, including computing hardware, potentially exceeding $500 billion. The first phase is expected to become operational later this decade. Rather than directly funding construction, Nvidia is said to be considering financial guarantees that would improve borrowing conditions for the project. Also, Nvidia and South Korea's SK Group announced an AI partnership worth more than $500 billion, in which SK Hynix (SKHY) will work with Nvidia to supply next-generation memory chips and jointly develop high-bandwidth memory (HBM) for AI training, AI agents and physical AI applications. Nvidia stock gained nearly 2% last week. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around the stock remained in ‘neutral’ territory. Alphabet Inc. (GOOGL) posted another quarter of strong revenue growth while highlighting ambitious development plans for Gemini AI models. The company raised its 2026 capital spending forecast to $195 billion-$205 billion, reflecting continued heavy investment in AI infrastructure. Investors are watching closely to see if Google’s heavy AI investments will generate enough returns. Google Cloud revenue rose to $24.77 billion, while Alphabet’s total revenue reached $119.8 billion, both exceeding Street expectations. Alphabet said its Gemini AI service now has 950 million monthly users, and Google Cloud’s order backlog increased to $514 billion, showing strong demand for AI services from businesses. Alphabet stock tumbled over 7% during the week. Retail sentiment around the stock remained in ‘extremely bullish’ territory. Tesla Inc. (TSLA) stock took a beating, plunging 17% over the week as the company reported weaker earnings despite higher revenue and strong vehicle deliveries. Tesla's second-quarter revenue rose to $28.2 billion, beating expectations, helped by record vehicle deliveries and strong energy storage sales. However, adjusted earnings per share dropped to $0.55, below analyst forecasts and lower than the same period last year. The company also reported negative free cash flow of $1.1 billion as it increased spending on AI, robotics and new products. Capital spending jumped 142% to $5.8 billion in the quarter as Tesla prepares for projects including its Optimus humanoid robot, Semi truck and Cybercab robotaxi. Retail sentiment around the stock remained in ‘neutral’ territory. Oracle Corp. (ORCL) secured a nearly $7 billion, 10-year software agreement with the U.S. Defense Department. The agreement covers Oracle’s software used in government data centers supporting military branches, intelligence agencies and the Coast Guard. The initial five-year portion of the deal is valued at $3.31 billion and includes software licenses, maintenance, support and consulting services. The contract aims to simplify government software purchasing by bringing multiple Oracle agreements under one larger arrangement. However, Oracle stock recorded a weekly decline of 9% and retail sentiment around the stock remained in ‘bullish’ territory. Intel Corp. (INTC) reported a 25% increase in Q2 revenue to $16.1 billion, beating analyst expectations, while adjusted earnings also came in above forecasts. The company’s data center business was a major driver, with sales jumping 59% to $6.3 billion during the quarter. The chipmaker also raised its capital spending plans to $20 billion this year as it invests in manufacturing and its foundry business. CEO Lip-Bu Tan said demand for data center processors is growing faster than supply. Intel stock dropped 2% during the week with retail sentiment remaining in ‘extremely bullish’ territory. Comcast Corp. (CMCSA), Verizon Communications Inc. (VZ), T-Mobile US Inc. (TMUS), AT&T Inc. (T) and Nokia Corp. (NOK) also reported earnings, reflecting resilient demand alongside continued pressure on consumer spending and equipment sales.
